4.9: The place of production proved influential for nearly every trait determined. Birbhum and Howrah returned the best milling percentage, head rice recovery, total phenol, total flavonoid, antioxidant capacity, iron and phytic acid; Nadia the best hulling, soluble protein, fat, copper and zinc; and Purba Bardhaman the weakest values for the majority of traits determining nutritional value. Kalojira emerged as the superior all-round landrace, Gobindabhog as the better source of soluble protein, grain shape, iron and thirteen of the fifteen amino acids, and Radhunipagal as highest for zinc alone. Storage acted in two opposing directions concurrently: head rice recovery gained 2.13 percentage points up to 8 months and amylose increased by 12.8% over the year, whereas aroma declined by 31.7%, soluble protein by 41.4%, fat by 31.3%, total phenol by 52.4%, total flavonoid by 37.3% and antioxidant capacity by 62.7%. The four minerals remained unchanged while phytic acid declined by 40.0%, so that the phytate to mineral balance improved with ageing. A storage period of four to eight months represents the optimal compromise for these landraces.
4.21: In the four cooked products the cultivars differed significantly for nearly all the attributes determined, whereas year and its interaction with cultivar were significant for considerably fewer, so that the choice of cultivar determines product quality and a cultivar selected on one year of results will generally retain its position in the next. On the composite index the superior cultivar was Kalojira for table rice, Radhunipagal for khichdi, Kataribhog for pulao and Gobindabhog for payash, the control ranking at or near the bottom in every product (Table 4.67). Weights derived independently from principal component analysis reproduced the ranking, with a mean Spearman correlation of 0.942, a minimum of 0.867 and the same cultivar first in 3 of the 4 products (Table 4.69). Ward clustering of the 40 cultivar and product combinations yielded 4 groups, 3 of them containing a single product only (Table 4.70 and Fig. 4.31): the preparation fixes the type of product and the cultivar its standing within that type.
4.31: In the three processed products the cultivars again differed significantly for nearly all the attributes determined, whereas year and its interaction with cultivar were significant for considerably fewer. On the composite index the superior cultivar was Gobindabhog for popped rice, Radhatilak for puffed rice and Harinakhuri for flattened rice, the control ranking at or near the bottom in every product (Table 4.95). Weights derived independently from principal component analysis reproduced the ranking, with a mean Spearman correlation of 0.952, a minimum of 0.939 and the same cultivar first in 3 of the 3 products (Table 4.97). Ward clustering of the 30 cultivar and product combinations yielded 3 groups, 2 of them containing a single product only (Table 4.98 and Fig. 4.55), confirming that the preparation fixes the type of product while the cultivar determines its standing within that type.
4.32: Across the seven products the cultivars differed significantly for nearly every attribute determined, whereas the year of production and its interaction with cultivar were significant for considerably fewer, so that the identity of the cultivar governs the quality of the finished product. On the composite quality score index the superior cultivar was Gobindabhog for payash and popped rice, Kalojira for table rice, Radhunipagal for khichdi, Kataribhog for pulao, Radhatilak for puffed rice and Harinakhuri for flattened rice, the non-aromatic control ranking at or near the foot of the order in every product. No single cultivar proved superior for all seven, so that the choice of raw material must follow the product intended. Weights derived from principal component analysis reproduced the ranking, the mean rank correlation being 0.946 with the same cultivar first in 6 of the seven, and clustering yielded 7 groups across the two parts, 5 of them containing a single product only. The cultivars identified should be re-evaluated over additional years before any general recommendation is advanced.
4.43: Variety, type of fortification and their interaction all exerted a significant effect on the quality of idli prepared from aromatic rice, fortification proving the stronger factor and being identified by both the principal component analysis and the cluster analysis as the principal source of variation. The three aromatic landraces were superior to the non-aromatic control for protein, phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant potential and every sensory attribute, Kalojira being richest in the bioactive fractions, Gobindabhog richest in minerals with the lowest phytate, and Radhunipagal yielding the softest product. Beet extract elevated phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant activity, calcium and anthocyanin, while carrot extract supplied β-carotene and yielded the highest resistant starch with the lowest glycaemic index. KBI is therefore recommended as the superior combination, KCI where a provitamin A-rich product of low glycaemic response is required, and GBI where a mineral-enriched product is required.
